sourceDesc.p: The collectives Cavriana writes about: peoples, confessions, and bodies of soldiers. He very often reports on groups rather than on named men, and those passages were invisible to an index built only of persons and places.

p.bibl: A group that stands for a country carries a pointer to that place, so "i Corsi" counts towards Corsica and appears on the map. A group defined by belief or by trade — the Huguenots, the reiters — points nowhere on a map, and is recorded here alone.
The characterisations are drafted from the letters themselves and describe how Cavriana presents each group, not what the group was.

personGrp.note: The most named group in the correspondence. Cavriana writes of them as a party with a military and a political existence at once: they hold places of safety, they levy reiters they cannot pay, they send deputies to negotiate, and they are watched for what they will do when the peace is executed. He does not write of them as heretics; the vocabulary is of strength, credit and intention.

Named a third as often as the Huguenots, and almost always in the same breath as them: what the Catholics will accept, where they will not have the edict executed, which towns refuse to readmit the banished. Cavriana treats them as the other party to a settlement rather than as the religion of the kingdom.

German horse in French service, and in these letters a question of money before anything else. They march slowly towards the frontier because those who owe them are slow to pay; four hundred thousand francs a year are promised for them. Cavriana reports them as an instrument that both sides hire and neither can afford.
Named with the Turks as what occupies Spain elsewhere, and so as a reason the Spanish cannot pursue their designs in Europe undisturbed.
Named once, in August 1570, as what a foreign war would purge from France: the kingdom is to be cleansed of its bandits and idle men by carrying the arms elsewhere.
